TO THE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
Judy Graci, Pro se intervenor, files this response under SOAH Order No. 35 to the Applicants’ Brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13, filed October 7, 2026 (the “Applicants’ Brief”). The Applicants’ Brief attaches and incorporates the Applicants’ Directory of Record Evidence (the “Directory”) as Exhibit A. Ms. Graci incorporates her October 7, 2026 brief (the “Graci Brief”). As there, “Import Path 2” or “the Project” refers to both halves of Import Path 2: the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation line (Docket No. 59475) and the Big Hill Substation to Sand Lake Switch line (Docket No. 59182).
I.  SUMMARY OF RESPONSE
The Applicants’ Brief does not answer the PFD’s findings that no study justified Import Path 2 individually and that NERC contingencies are not a substitute for project-specific need. It says Import Path 2 and “the other PBRP projects” together resolve the violations, which is the package-wide showing the PFD found insufficient.
The Applicants ask the ALJs to adopt findings from the Commission’s orders in other dockets. Those orders are not on this evidentiary record, which the ALJs will not reopen.
The “multiple independent studies” are not independent. The Applicants concede the later planning models assume Import Path 2 is in service, and they identify no study that tests the system without it.
Commission Staff’s brief adapts the Applicants’ position. It quotes the Applicants’ exceptions, cites the Directory only “generally,” and does not address the PFD’s findings on project-specific need, load, or generation.
Issue 13. The Applicants concede they were not required to show congestion cost savings and offer no estimate. They do not dispute the PFD’s findings that no estimate was submitted and that the record contains no evidence quantifying one. Because the record will not be reopened, the only supportable finding is that it establishes no estimate of savings.
The exemption of PBRP projects from further RPG review, even if within the Commission’s authority under PURA §§ 39.166-.167, did not satisfy the separate necessity determination under PURA § 37.056 or relieve the Applicants of their burden.
The admitted record does not substantiate the PBRP modeling on which the reliability conclusion depends. The Applicants’ discovery responses show they lack the PBRP’s load, generation and power-flow inputs, and they concede the PBRP added only about 17,170 MW of generation and used 2023 load data outside West Texas, while the 2024 RTP contained materially more load and generation.
II. ISSUE 11: THE APPLICANTS’ BRIEF DOES NOT SHOW THAT IMPORT PATH 2 IS NECESSARY TO MEET A RELIABILITY STANDARD
A.  Findings from other dockets are not evidence in this record.
The Applicants propose that the supplemental PFD adopt “findings of fact already adopted” in the Commission’s orders approving Import Path 1 (Dockets 59315 and 59029) and Import Path 3 (Docket 59336). Order No. 35 states that the ALJs will not reopen the evidentiary record and that factual assertions must include pinpoint citations from the record. The Applicants cite no record exhibit for the Commission’s findings in those dockets. Findings in another proceeding are not evidence in this one, and a supplemental PFD must rest on the evidence admitted here. The Applicants have not asked for official notice of those orders or of their records.
Those dockets also concerned different facilities and different records. The Commission signed its order remanding this docket for further findings on Issues 11 and 13 on September 18, 2026, the same day it approved Import Path 3, and it did not approve Import Path 2.
The proposed findings also conflict with the PFD and with each other. One proposed finding says ERCOT evaluated several alternatives and found none more efficient. Another, in the same list, says the Applicants “did not independently evaluate alternatives.” The PFD notes that Applicants were exempted from further RPG review, and it found credible evidence relevant to alternatives, namely new and planned Permian Basin gas generation, that the Commission should consider. The proposed findings that distribution alternatives would not work, and that adding transformers, raising voltages or bundling conductors “would also fail,” have no record citation in the Applicants’ Brief.
B.  The “multiple independent studies” assume the answer.
The Applicants say the PBRP, the 2024 RTP, the 2025 RTP and the April 2026 GTC exit strategy each independently found Import Path 2 necessary. The Applicants’ Brief itself states that the 2024 and 2025 RTPs “assume the Import Path 2 Projects are in service,” and that the 2025 RTP put all three paths in its starting cases “to address base case violations.” A study that assumes the facility is built shows how the system performs with it, not whether it is necessary. The question on remand is whether the existing record establishes that Import Path 2 itself is necessary, not merely whether the system performs better when the project is assumed in service. The Applicants’ Brief then says the record contains no study modeling a reliable alternative with those facilities removed. That is the gap, not an answer to it.
The April 2026 GTC exit strategy does not fill it. The PFD found that the Far West Import GTCs have not resulted in any load shed to date, that ERCOT lists the 765-kV paths as one of seven upgrades that “help” exit the GTCs, that GTCs do not validate the load behind them, and that they do not validate the PBRP load forecast or the necessity of Import Path 2. The Applicants’ description of the GTCs as a problem “on the grid today” does not engage those findings. The Applicants also say all three paths are essential even if about 2,500 MW of planned generation materializes. The PFD found 24 gas projects totaling 25.162 GW in the Permian Basin alone, about ten times that figure, being developed at a scale that rivals or exceeds the PBRP’s projected load. The assumption behind the exit strategy is outdated on this record.
C.  The Applicants’ Brief shifts the burden and misreads the testimony.
The Applicants say “no independent analysis or planning study” shows the plan would still resolve the violations without Import Path 2, and call removing a component “ad hoc.” Issue 11 asks whether “the proposed transmission facilities” are necessary. The Applicants bear the burden of showing necessity, and the PFD found that they performed no partial-build study and did not establish need for Import Path 2 apart from the three-path project. The Applicants’ own conclusion that the violations are resolved by Import Path 2 “together with the other PBRP projects” confirms the showing is package-wide.
The Applicants also write that, “As Mr. Gurley testified, ERCOT studied the paths together because” TPL-001-5.1 requires N-1 and N-1-1 studies. The transcript does not say that. Mr. Gurley said he was not aware of a study that isolated each line and that the paths “were studied together.” His explanation about TPL-001 followed the words “I assume.” An assumption by the witness is not testimony about what ERCOT did or why.
D.  The PFD’s Finding of Fact No. 224 is accurate.
The Applicants call Finding of Fact No. 224 “flatly incorrect” because the Project will operate in both directions. The finding does not say the lines cannot carry power east. It says the Applicants present the Project as one that will import power westward into the Permian Basin, not as one necessary to meet a reliability standard. The Applicants’ Brief confirms the framing: it describes the need as importing power to serve load and calls importing power and resolving overloads “two sides of the same coin.” That does not identify a standard the system would violate without Import Path 2. The export and curtailment benefit the Applicants add are economic benefits, which they say are “additional value,” not a basis for need.
E.  Great weight does not make the recommendation conclusive.
The Applicants say each ERCOT recommendation is “independently” entitled to great weight, and that the ALJs are “required” to give it great evidentiary weight. The Applicants’ Brief does not mention the PFD’s findings that the PBRP recommendation relies on a load forecast ERCOT’s own 2025 methodology cut materially, that it should not be given great weight, and that even with great weight the greater weight of credible evidence is against it. Deference to ERCOT’s expertise does not substitute for evidence that Import Path 2 is necessary.
F.  The exemption of PBRP projects from RPG review did not relieve the Applicants of their burden under PURA § 37.056.
The Applicants ask the ALJs to find that the Commission exempted the approved PBRP projects from further Regional Planning Group review, and that the Applicants did not independently evaluate alternatives. The Applicants’ position is that the exemption also settles Issue 11. It does not. Ms. Graci does not ask the ALJs to decide whether PURA §§ 39.166-.167 authorized the Commission to exempt individual PBRP projects from the otherwise applicable ERCOT Regional Planning Group (RPG) project-review process. The ALJs can assume that it did.
Even on that assumption, the exemption was a decision about what must happen before a CCN application is filed. It did not amend PURA § 37.056, and it did not satisfy the separate necessity determination that statute requires. Section 37.056 makes the grant of a certificate depend on findings made in the CCN proceeding itself, as the Commission’s own orders and the PFD recognize, including a finding that the facilities are necessary and a consideration of the need for additional service. The Applicants’ own Brief says an affirmative answer on Issue 11 “informs” the need analysis under PURA § 37.056(c)(1)-(2) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii), which concedes that the need analysis is still required. A decision to skip one review step before filing does not decide that question, and the remand of this docket for further findings on Issues 11 and 13 confirms that necessity remains open.
The same is true of alternatives. Being excused from an RPG alternatives analysis is not the same as showing, in this proceeding, that no reasonable alternative exists. The alternatives the Applicants point to are the 345-, 500- and 765-kV options for the import paths, which compare voltage levels for the same paths and are not alternatives to building import paths at all. As Part II.A notes, the PFD found credible evidence of an alternative, new and planned Permian Basin gas generation. The exemption removed a step from the process. It did not remove the Applicants’ burden to prove necessity on this record. The Commission’s Project No. 55718 order makes the distinction explicit: Ordering Paragraph 10 requires the applicable TSP to establish in the CCN proceeding that its certificate satisfies all applicable legal requirements, including PURA § 37.056(a), while Ordering Paragraph 11 provides only that the approved PBRP projects do not require additional ERCOT RPG review before a CCN application may be filed. The Commission’s own Project No. 55718 order expressly required each TSP to establish in the CCN proceeding that its certificate satisfies applicable legal requirements, including PURA § 37.056(a), while separately stating that the approved PBRP projects did not require additional ERCOT RPG review before a CCN application could be filed.
G.  The record does not substantiate the modeling on which the reliability conclusion depends.
Issue 11 asks whether the existing record shows that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet a reliability standard. The Applicants’ answer rests on ERCOT’s PBRP modeling of load, generation and system power flows, which they filed as Attachment 5 to the Application. This Part relies only on evidence already admitted and on the PFD’s findings.
The admitted record shows that the Applicants did not build that model and do not have its inputs. Asked in discovery by Intervenor Kevin Kennedy to describe their engineering knowledge of the PBRP modeling, the Applicants answered that, although they provided input to ERCOT on methodology and assumptions, it was ERCOT, not the Applicants, that performed the study, and they referred to the study itself. Asked for the load-demand and future-generation data behind each 765-kV load case, the Applicants answered that they do not have that data beyond what appears in the PBRP, and that ERCOT developed the cases and performed the studies. The same request also asked for the rate and direction of power flow on each of the five 765-kV import path links. The response gives none. Asked whether the PBRP model had the same geographic boundary as the 2024 and 2025 RTP models, they answered that they do not have that information because ERCOT performed the studies, and that, based on the study reports, all of the cases contained the entire ERCOT system. These are admitted responses, not new facts. They do not prove the model is wrong. They show that the Applicants, who carry the burden, cannot supply the load, generation or power-flow data behind the PBRP’s conclusion beyond what the PBRP report itself contains.
The PBRP’s load assumptions were also challenged in this record, and the ALJs agreed. The PFD found the PBRP load forecast overstated and unverified, found that ERCOT’s own 2025 methodology cut it materially, and found that it should not receive great weight. The Applicants’ proposed load findings only recite what ERCOT modeled, 23,659 MW for 2030 and 26,400 MW for 2038, and a recital of what was modeled is not a finding that the load is real. A reliability study is only as sound as the load it assumes. If the load is overstated, the flows and violations the model reports are overstated with it.
The 2024 RTP is also in the record and gives a way to test the PBRP’s assumptions. It is in evidence as an attachment to Mr. Gurley’s rebuttal testimony. The two documents report very different amounts of added generation: about 59,200 MW in Appendix B to the 2024 RTP, and about 17,170 MW in Appendix A.1 to the PBRP. The difference is roughly 42,000 MW. The Applicants’ discovery responses show they do not have the data to reconcile the two, and they point to no record testimony that does. Their response to Mr. Kennedy’s appeal instead concedes the facts that create the gap. They do not dispute that the PBRP case added only about 17,170 MW of new generation. They say the 2024 RTP updated load, generation and topology across the entire ERCOT system and therefore contained materially more new statewide load and associated generation than the PBRP case. And they say the load outside West Texas in the PBRP was based on 2023 RTP load data. These are admissions by the party with the burden. The Applicants’ remaining answer, that the two studies had different purposes, is argument and not evidence, and it does not show that leaving that load and generation out did not matter to the flows on Import Path 2. Ms. Graci does not ask the ALJs to decide which model is right. The point is that the record contains no evidence showing that a gap of this size did not matter.
The statute and Commission rule point in the same direction. PURA § 37.056(c-1) requires the Commission, when considering the need for additional service for an ERCOT reliability transmission project, to consider historical load, forecasted load growth, and additional load currently seeking interconnection. The Commission’s rule likewise requires those factors to be incorporated into ERCOT reliability review and requires forecasted load growth and additional load currently seeking interconnection to be substantiated by quantifiable evidence. A reliability conclusion built on a load forecast the ALJs found overstated and unverified, run through a model whose inputs the Applicants cannot describe and whose results the record does not reconcile with the 2024 RTP, is not the showing the rule describes.
The question on remand is whether the existing evidentiary record supports the reliability conclusion. ERCOT’s recommendation, though entitled to great weight, does not answer it, as Part II.E explains. For the reasons above, the existing record does not establish that the PBRP modeling underlying Import Path 2 reliably shows the project is necessary under Issue 11.
III. ISSUE 13: THE APPLICANTS’ BRIEF OFFERS NO ESTIMATE OF CONSUMER SAVINGS FROM IMPORT PATH 2
A.  The Applicants concede no estimate was required and do not dispute the PFD’s findings.
The Applicants agree that the PFD “correctly recognized” that a congestion cost savings analysis is not required for reliability projects, and they say they “were not required to demonstrate” savings. They do not dispute that they submitted no estimate of the cost to consumers or of congestion cost savings, or that the record contains no evidence quantifying either. They ask only that the PFD “additionally acknowledge” benefits. Benefits that are not quantified as savings from Import Path 2 are not the estimate Issue 13 asks for.
B.  The figures the Applicants offer compare plans and do not isolate Import Path 2.
The Applicants’ savings figures, 1,443 miles of avoided upgrades, $890 million in outage-related construction costs and annual cost savings, are stated “compared with a 345 kV alternative.” That compares one build plan to another. It does not estimate savings from Import Path 2 against not building it, and the compared 765-kV plan covers the statewide plan, not Import Path 2 alone.
The headline figure is also incomplete. The Applicants’ Brief gives the $229 million consumer energy cost saving as an “annual” amount without a year. In JG-4 that figure is the 2039 result. For 2034 the same table shows an incremental consumer energy cost benefit of negative $136 million for the 765-kV plan against the 345-kV plan. The Applicants’ Brief also gives two totals, “over $270 million” in annual savings and $229 million plus $28 million and cites the same two pages of Mr. Gurley’s testimony for both.
The Applicants also repeat the Independent Market Monitor’s estimate that congestion cost ratepayers over $10 billion from 2020 through 2024, about $3 billion of it in West Texas. That is a historical statewide total. It is not an estimate of what Import Path 2 would save, and it does not account for the PFD’s finding that the load forecast driving future congestion is overstated. 
C.  The finding the Applicants request is not supported.
The Applicants ask for a finding that “the record nonetheless shows” substantial benefits to consumers. The record shows plan-level modeling against a 345-kV alternative, mixed results across the years the Applicants chose, and historical statewide totals.
D.  The record cannot be reopened, so the only supportable finding is that it establishes no estimate of savings.
Order No. 35 states that the ALJs will not reopen the evidentiary record. The existing record contains no quantified estimate of the congestion cost savings to consumers from Import Path 2, and the data needed to calculate one was requested and not produced. Intervenor Kevin Kennedy asked the Applicants for the rate and direction of power flow on each of the five 765-kV import path links for every 765-kV load case modeled in the PBRP and in the 2024 RTP. Any estimate of what Import Path 2 would save in congestion costs would have to start from those flows. The Applicants’ responses provided no flow data. For the PBRP, they said they do not have the load and generation data beyond what is in the PBRP, and that ERCOT performed the studies. For the 2024 RTP, they said ERCOT developed it and referred to ERCOT’s public report.
The Applicants therefore cannot attribute congestion relief, or consumer savings, to Import Path 2, and the plan-level figures in JG-4 do not isolate it. Because the record will not be reopened to add what was not produced, the only defensible finding on Issue 13 is that the existing record does not establish any estimate of consumer congestion cost savings from Import Path 2. That matches FOF Nos. 226-227 and is consistent with the Applicants’ position that they were not required to show savings. It does not say savings are impossible. It says none were proven on this record.
IV. COMMISSION STAFF’S BRIEF
Staff recommend that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet reliability standards and therefore qualifies as a reliability project. Staff’s Issue 11 argument adopts the Applicants’ position. It quotes the Applicants’ exceptions to the PFD, which are argument and not evidence, and it cites the Directory only “generally,” at pages 3-15. A citation to the Directory at pages 3-15 does not provide the pinpoint citation required by Order No. 35. The one record cite Staff gives for ERCOT’s studies is Staff witness Poole’s direct testimony at 26:3-11, which Staff describes as ERCOT’s conclusion that a 765-kV backbone is needed to increase import capability into the Permian Basin. That is a regional conclusion, not a finding that Import Path 2 individually is necessary.
Staff does not address the PFD’s findings that no study justified Import Path 2 individually, that the PBRP load forecast is overstated and should not receive great weight, or that new Permian Basin generation is being developed at a scale that rivals or exceeds the projected load. Staff’s own witness agreed on cross-examination that the methodology behind the load forecast needs to change. Staff’s reliance on the 2024 RTP, the 2025 RTP and the GTC exit strategy repeats the Applicants’ argument, and it fails for the reasons in Part II.B.
On Issue 13, Staff agrees that no congestion cost savings analysis is required for a reliability project, which is consistent with the PFD. Staff offers figures only “to the extent” the ALJs disagree. Its own figures, taken from JG-4, are consumer energy cost savings against the base case of $0.199 billion for the 345-kV plan and $0.063 billion for the 765-kV plan in 2034, and $0.156 billion for the 765-kV plan alone in 2039. Staff thus concedes the 345-kV plan saves consumers more in 2034. All these figures are for the whole statewide plan, and Staff does not attribute any portion to Import Path 2. ERCOT’s estimated cost of the 765-kV plan in its reduced-load sensitivity case is $23.91 billion.
Staff then reasons that reduced congestion rent, together with added capacity, “indicate” that the 765-kV plan “will help reduce” congestion costs for consumers. That is an inference. It is not an estimate of savings from Import Path 2, and Staff does not convert congestion rent into a consumer savings figure. Staff’s support for annual congestion costs in the area is the Applicants’ post-hearing brief, which is argument, citing testimony that describes congestion in general terms. Staff’s closing statement that Import Path 2 is “supported from an economic standpoint” also conflicts with the Applicants’ position that it is not justified on economic criteria.
V. CONCLUSION AND PRAYER
Ms. Graci respectfully requests that the ALJs (1) decline to adopt the findings of fact the Applicants propose from other dockets and the finding that the Project is necessary to meet state and federal reliability standards, and decline Commission Staff’s recommendation to the same effect; (2) find, consistent with Finding of Fact Nos. 128-131, that the Applicants have not shown Import Path 2 is necessary to meet a reliability standard, that the exemption of PBRP projects from RPG review did not relieve the Applicants of their burden under PURA § 37.056, and that the existing record, including the Applicants’ admitted responses to Kennedy Exs. N15, N20 and N23, does not establish that the PBRP modeling reliably shows Import Path 2 is necessary (Issue 11); (3) find, consistent with Finding of Fact Nos. 226-227, that the record contains no estimate of the congestion cost savings to consumers from Import Path 2 and, because the record will not be reopened, does not establish any estimated consumer congestion cost savings from Import Path 2 (Issue 13); and (4) adopt the findings requested in the Graci Brief and recommend that the Commission deny both Applications.
Respectfully submitted,
